title: Benedict: pray and work
hook: the Rule of Benedict balances prayer, work and rest in community (Rule 48)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Nyssa's endless climb. Your line was always further in. Did you take one more step? Day two hundred sixty-six, the end of the week.

Most of us live with a split down the middle. There's the spiritual part of life: church, prayer, the quiet ten minutes if we're lucky. And then there's everything else. Emails, laundry, the commute, the spreadsheet, the dishes. The two feel like different worlds, and the second one takes up almost all the hours. Around fifteen hundred years ago, a monk in Italy wrote a little rulebook for his community, and one of the things it quietly does is erase that split. Prayer has its hours. Work has its hours. And both belong to God. Today's word is the famous summary of his Rule: ora et labora.
screen: `TWO WORLDS.` → `A LITTLE RULEBOOK.` → `BOTH BELONG TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Benedict of Nursia lived in the late 400s and early 500s, as the old Roman world was falling apart. Tradition says he first lived alone in a cave, then gathered monks together, and founded a monastery at Monte Cassino. For them he wrote the Rule of Saint Benedict, about seventy short chapters on how to live together. Its very first word is listen. The Rule sets the day by the bells: prayer together, seven times in the day and once in the night. And in between, work: in the fields, the kitchen, the workshop. And reading, slow reading of scripture. Chapter forty-eight begins with a line in Latin that monks have quoted ever since: otiositas inimica est animae, idleness is the enemy of the soul. Then it lays out the hours for work and the hours for reading, season by season. Now a surprise. The words ora et labora, pray and work, are not actually in the Rule. They're a later motto, a summary people made of it. But it's a fair one. And the Rule goes further than balance. In one chapter, Benedict tells the monk who looks after the kitchen and storeroom to treat every tool and pot of the monastery as if it were a sacred vessel of the altar. The bread knife and the chalice, handled with the same care. That's what pray and work really means. Not prayer, and then the real stuff. Work done as prayer. For fifteen centuries, Benedictine monks and nuns have lived by this Rule, and many people outside monasteries, Catholic, Anglican and others, use it as a guide for ordinary life. This week took us from the house on the rock to the desert and the cell. Benedict brings the desert indoors, into a kitchen.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.` · `IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.` · `THE MOTTO ISN'T IN THE RULE.` · `THE POT AND THE CHALICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next piece of work waiting for you today. Maybe it's typing, maybe it's cooking, maybe it's cleaning up after someone. Picture the tools you'll use: the keyboard, the pan, the sponge. Picture handling them carefully, the way you'd handle something precious. If you pray, you can offer the work before you start it. The bell holds the time.
Ora et labora. Latin: pray and work. A later motto, but a true summary of Benedict's Rule.
Your line: pray and work. Today, do one ordinary task slowly and carefully, as if the tools were sacred. Day two hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying together at set hours and working in between, and many lay Christians, called oblates, follow the Rule in their own homes and jobs.

original.note: Latin: pray and work; a later motto summing up Benedict's Rule.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks pray, and someone else does the work.
what it means: prayer and work share the day, and the work is done as prayer.
what a scholar hears: otiositas inimica est animae (Rule 48); the kitchen tools as altar vessels (Rule 31); and a motto that appears nowhere in the Rule itself.

notes: The Latin 'otiositas inimica est animae' (RB 48.1) is given in the original and translated; confirm.
RB 16 counts seven day hours and the night office; RB 31.10 asks the cellarer to regard all utensils as sacred vessels of the altar. Paraphrased; confirm.
'Ora et labora' as a later (often said nineteenth-century) motto not found in the Rule: confirm wording.
Benedict's biography (cave at Subiaco, Monte Cassino) comes from Gregory the Great's Dialogues; the script says 'tradition says'.
